CausalChain: COL1A2 upregulation -> Enhanced integrin signaling (via FAK/PI3K-AKT and MAPK cascades) -> Phosphorylation/modification of mRNA export regulators (e.g., XPO1, RNA-binding proteins) -> Selective enhanced mRNA export of oncogenic transcripts -> Increased metastasis and angiogenesis -> Poorer liver neoplasm prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, elevated COL1A2 expression not only drives extracellular matrix remodeling but also instigates a specific intracellular signaling cascade. This cascade, initiated by enhanced integrin engagement, activates kinase pathways (FAK/PI3K-AKT and MAPK) which phosphorylate and thereby modulate the activity of mRNA export regulators such as XPO1 and certain RNA-binding proteins. The resulting post-translational modifications selectively boost the export and translation of oncogenic mRNAs, ultimately leading to increased tumor metastasis and angiogenesis. This refined mechanism will be explored through the application of CRISPR-based gene editing and quantitative phosphoproteomics, providing a robust and technologically-advanced framework to validate the interplay between the ECM and nuclear export in liver neoplasm progression.
Abstract: In liver neoplasms, we propose that the overexpression of COL1A2 not only remodels the extracellular matrix but also triggers a cascade of intracellular events leading to enhanced oncogenic mRNA export. Specifically, COL1A2 upregulation boosts integrin signaling, which in turn activates key kinase cascades such as FAK/PI3K-AKT and MAPK. These cascades promote post-translational modifications—particularly phosphorylation—of critical mRNA export regulators including XPO1 and associated RNA-binding proteins. The modified export machinery selectively increases the nuclear export and subsequent translation of oncogenic transcripts, thereby promoting metastasis, angiogenesis, and ultimately leading to poorer clinical outcomes. Our hypothesis will be tested using cutting-edge technologies such as CRISPR-mediated gene modulation and mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics to elucidate the precise molecular intermediates linking ECM dynamics to nuclear export regulation.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed a link between COL1A2 upregulation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and enhanced mRNA export via integrin signaling without specifying the underlying signaling intermediates. The revised hypothesis retains the core idea but adds specificity by detailing the involvement of FAK/PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways that mediate phosphorylation events on nuclear export regulators such as XPO1. Moreover, the new formulation incorporates contemporary technologies like CRISPR-based gene modulation and mass spectrometry phosphoproteomics to experimentally validate the causal chain, thereby enhancing both the mechanistic clarity and practical implementability of the hypothesis.
